routes.description: Establish that the surviving witness tradition and comparative methods preserve the New Testament's wording to a sufficiently high, historically appropriate degree of probability for the text to be trusted, despite localized uncertainty and the loss of the autographs.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if cumulative manuscript evidence and reconstructive method justify substantial recovery under a probabilistic standard, while the remaining meaningful variants are shown to be limited enough that local uncertainty does not defeat trust in the text as a whole.

motionBridge.description: Connect substantial probabilistic recovery, rather than certainty at every disputed reading, to the level of confidence required to trust the New Testament text.

centralBridges.description: Show that numerous, early, geographically or genealogically independent manuscripts, versions, and patristic witnesses provide cumulative access to earlier textual states.
Explain how comparison across branching written witnesses can identify copying errors and reconstruct ancestral wording even when the autographs and earliest copies are unavailable.
Establish that most variants are insignificant or readily identifiable and that the smaller set of meaningful viable disputes does not prevent substantial textual recovery.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply concrete evidence of careful early transmission or agreement between early witnesses that supports stability before the principal surviving codices.
Justify probability rather than absolute certainty as the appropriate standard for historical trust and relate the available evidence to ordinary work on ancient texts.

routes.description: Establish that textual criticism may recover an ancestral form behind the surviving witnesses without providing enough evidence to identify that form confidently with the authors' original wording, making the requested level of textual trust unwarranted.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the undocumented earliest transmission period leaves a material possibility of consequential changes shared by all surviving branches, and if later abundance, reconstructive success, or broad continuity cannot close that evidentiary gap to the autograph.

motionBridge.description: Connect the unresolved gap between the earliest reconstructable text and the authorial wording to the conclusion that confidence sufficient for the motion has not been established.

centralBridges.description: Show that the loss of the autographs and earliest generations of copies prevents direct testing of copying accuracy during the period most capable of seeding every surviving branch.
Maintain the distinction between reconstructing the initial ancestor of extant witnesses and demonstrating that this reconstructed text is identical to the autograph.
Establish that scribal variation includes intentional, substantial, or interpretively consequential changes, so recoverable broad continuity does not resolve every material uncertainty.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why the quantity of predominantly later witnesses and the low proportion of significant extant variants do not reveal changes predating the earliest surviving evidence.
Specify why the advocate of trust must provide affirmative evidence of reliable early transmission rather than treat the absence of known total discontinuity as sufficient.

sections.title: The Standard for Recovery and Textual Trust
sections.rationale: This issue defines whether the motion requires autographic certainty or a historically reasonable degree of confidence, and therefore sets the burden against which manuscript evidence and residual uncertainty must be considered.

sections.title: The Undocumented Earliest Transmission Period
sections.rationale: The central historical dispute concerns whether missing originals and early copies leave an unbridgeable evidentiary gap or whether circulation patterns, early witnesses, versions, and patristic testimony support continuity with authorial wording.

sections.title: Reconstructing Earlier Texts from Surviving Witnesses
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether comparison among branching manuscript traditions can recover predecessor readings despite accumulated errors, and whether the earliest reconstructable text can be identified with the autograph.

sections.title: The Evidentiary Value of Manuscript Abundance and Date
sections.rationale: The number, age, independence, and coverage of surviving witnesses matter to whether the manuscript tradition provides effective cross-checks, while raising the question whether relative abundance establishes original wording.

sections.title: The Scale and Proportion of Textual Variation
sections.rationale: This issue separates the raw number of variants from the subset that is meaningful and viable, determining what the surviving variation establishes about the stability and recoverability of the text.

sections.title: Consequential Variants and the Scope of Trust
sections.rationale: Disputed readings and recognized additions test whether local uncertainty materially limits textual trust, including whether interpretive or doctrinal significance bears on confidence in the New Testament as a whole.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Repeated copying before the earliest surviving manuscripts could propagate inherited and new mistakes, while the missing intervening copies prevent direct reconstruction of that earliest transmission history.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Bart Ehrman immediately before this uninterrupted first-person opening presentation.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly develops the undocumented-early-copying premise and therefore requires no opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly develops a central inferential premise with concrete historical framing.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The missing manuscripts warrant uncertainty about intervening copying, and the speaker expressly says the history is unknown rather than proving corruption.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from missing intervening copies to inability to inspect that transmission history is direct, with only the trust consequence left for later argument.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The dates and absence of intervening witnesses specifically support the evidentiary gap, though no comparative transmission model is developed here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It squarely supports the central early-gap bridge and occupies the top of that burden-contact tier.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The New Testament's unusually large number of surviving manuscripts does not resolve the absence of the early copies needed to test whether later witnesses preserve the original wording.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage continues Ehrman's uninterrupted opening statement after his transmission-history explanation.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman

moves.attributionBasis: The same identified speaker continues continuously, using John Mill's edition and current manuscript totals as supporting examples.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it supplies relevant scale evidence but does not itself establish the significance of those differences.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The inability to give a complete count is well framed, though categorical language about nobody knowing exceeds the limited counting history supplied.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The historical increase in manuscripts supports an expanding count, but raw uncounted quantity alone does not establish consequential uncertainty.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: John Mill and the expansion from roughly one hundred to thousands of manuscripts provide concrete support, with no counting methodology supplied.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Most surviving manuscript differences are insignificant accidental mistakes that trained critics can usually recognize, so the material dispute concerns the smaller set of consequential or difficult readings.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman's uninterrupted opening statement explicitly classifies the previously discussed manuscript differences and explains their significance.

response.rationale: This constructive classification concedes that most variants are accidental and recognizable while isolating the smaller material category.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it makes a clear and important distinction that narrows the genuine variant-scope dispute.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The assertion that accidental errors are usually recognizable is appropriately qualified and supported with ordinary copying examples.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the pro central variant-scope bridge despite being offered by con, and strongly narrows the relevant dispute.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move offers a classification and concession rather than testing a developed opposing interpretation.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Some scribal changes appear intentional and important, and the lack of witnesses from the earliest period prevents determining how many consequential changes arose there.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman explicitly introduces intentional changes as the next category within his continuous opening argument.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the consequential-change premise through intentional variants and uncertainty in the earliest period.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly develops a central burden, though its earliest-period extrapolation remains under-evidenced.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Possibility language appropriately marks unknown intentional changes, but the categorical comparison of early and later scribes lacks support in this excerpt.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The woman-taken-in-adultery narrative and Mark's longer ending are substantial, influential passages that entered the tradition later and are absent from the earliest manuscript evidence.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether missing early copies defeats historically sufficient trust, rather than merely eliminating certainty.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive availability question but does not fully establish independence or continuity back to each autograph.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The witness count and coverage are supported, but 'whole New Testament multiple times' compresses distribution and independence limitations.

charity.alternative: Most early witnesses are fragmentary and leave the first copying generations undocumented.

moves.speaker: Daniel B. Wallace
moves.proposition: Later New Testament manuscripts add only a limited amount of material to a substantially attested text, unlike many classical works surviving partially or across much larger gaps.
moves.attributionBasis: Wallace continues the same uninterrupted presentation, explicitly characterizing what skeptics infer from the dates of surviving manuscripts.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether later witnesses add useful evidence or merely multiply testimony too late to test the original.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it supplies material contrary evidence but leaves the decisive pre-survival limitation substantially unanswered.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Limited later growth is relevant, though treating two-percent accretion as broadly remarkable omits measurement and early-common-change caveats.

charity.alternative: Later stability cannot disclose changes already embedded in every surviving branch.
charity.decisiveQualification: Limited later accretion supports continuity only during the observable tradition, not necessarily to the autograph.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Observed limited later addition supports bounded later growth, but the inference toward original preservation leaves a material temporal bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The quantified two-percent claim is specific but its source, denominator, and treatment of substitutions or omissions are not defended here.

moves.speaker: Daniel B. Wallace

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive raw-scale inference very strongly but leaves the expressly isolated meaningful minority unresolved.

charity.alternative: Even a tiny percentage of a very large total can leave hundreds of consequential disputes.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move establishes the insignificance of the majority but does not eliminate the meaningful minority.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move validly distinguishes numerical prevalence from significance and supports that distinction with recognizable categories.

moves.attributionBasis: Wallace explicitly introduces the theological-beliefs question and attributes the supporting formulation to Ehrman during his uninterrupted speech.

moves.speaker: Daniel B. Wallace
moves.proposition: New Testament copying was not serial degradation because written branches, access to earlier witnesses, patristic commentary, and repeated consultation of originals supplied independent checks.
moves.attributionBasis: Wallace announces his first bottom-line argument and develops the transmission comparison continuously in his own first-person presentation.

components.text: The decisive inference treats repeated copying as a serial process in which errors simply accumulate beyond recovery.
The evidentiary value of multiple witnesses depends on their ability to provide cross-checking branches.

response.rationale: The move expressly diagnoses the serial-degradation model as inappropriate because copying is written and branching, critics can consult earlier witnesses, and patristic commentary supplies checks; the consequence is that accumulated errors need not make ancestral wording unrecoverable.

moves.proposition: Textual criticism can reconstruct the earliest text ancestral to the surviving witnesses without thereby establishing that this initial recoverable text is identical to the author's autograph.
moves.attributionBasis: An audience question addresses Ehrman, and the answer explicitly contrasts his position with Wallace's while discussing current textual-critical terminology.

components.text: The decisive inference moves from successful reconstruction of a surviving tradition's ancestor to recovery of the author's autograph.
The claim that an original reading survives among extant readings still requires identification of the tradition's ancestor with the autograph.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses the equivocation between the earliest reconstructable ancestor and the original text, notes current scholarly terminology, and states the defeating consequence that reconstruction alone does not prove autographic identity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly isolates the inferential gap and states exactly what successful reconstruction can and cannot establish.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between an Ausgangstext-like ancestral text and the author's original is the move's explicit and stable focus.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The logical requirement for an additional autograph-identification warrant is correctly stated without denying reconstructive success.

charity.alternative: Comparative criticism can reliably reconstruct the ancestor of the extant witnesses.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even full ancestral reconstruction does not, without further evidence, establish identity with the autograph.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction is explicit, internally consistent, and directly resolves the strongest validity challenge to equating reconstruction with originality.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Current research terminology and the defined reconstruction target support the distinction, though institutional practice is not independently documented here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly completes the central initial-autograph burden by identifying the indispensable inferential gap.

representationalCharity.rationale: The strongest pro methodological claim is granted before the precise additional inference is challenged.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says major European research centers have moved away from 'original text' terminology and instead reconstruct the text ancestral to surviving witnesses.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Having more New Testament manuscripts than survive for classical works makes comparative reconstruction easier but does not establish possession of the original New Testament text.
moves.attributionBasis: The audience question explicitly addresses Ehrman, and his answer acknowledges and then qualifies Wallace's manuscript comparison.

components.text: The decisive inference treats superiority to classical manuscript survival as evidence that the New Testament original is possessed.
More manuscripts can improve comparative reconstruction without independently identifying the autograph.
Later abundance and limited observed growth remain compatible with an earlier shared change.

response.rationale: The reply grants the comparative abundance and then expressly identifies why it does not entail possession of the original: quantity improves the comparative evidence base but leaves the autograph-identification question open.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it grants the premise, isolates the invalid comparative inference, and states the narrower consequence abundance supports.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between relative manuscript abundance, easier comparison, and possession of the original is explicit and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is a calibrated logical limitation: comparative abundance does not by itself entail autographic identity.

charity.alternative: The New Testament has far more manuscripts than major classical works, improving reconstruction.
charity.decisiveQualification: Improved comparative reconstruction does not alone demonstrate that the reconstructed text is the autograph.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reply cleanly distinguishes a comparative evidentiary advantage from the separate conclusion of autographic possession.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The opponent's comparative premise is granted, and the limiting inference is primarily logical rather than dependent on additional disputed facts.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central witnesses bridge at the point where witness quantity is connected to original wording.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply emphatically grants the strongest factual premise and challenges only its overextended consequence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt repeatedly grants that New Testament manuscripts far outnumber those for classical authors while denying that this numerical fact establishes the original text.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Historical probability makes total discontinuity between the surviving Gospel of Mark and Mark's writing unlikely, but it cannot determine exact identity or the extent of their differences.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Ehrman's closing statement, and the first-person closing argument continues without a speaker change.

components.text: The decisive demand is what degree of probabilistic continuity the surviving text supports without exact autographic knowledge.
Locating an ancestral reading among manuscripts does not determine exact identity with Mark's wording.

response.rationale: The reply accepts historical probability and rejects total discontinuity while preserving uncertainty about exact wording and difference magnitude, directly engaging rather than evading the proposed relative-confidence standard.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the probabilistic standard and gives a nuanced consequence for both broad continuity and exact identity.

precisionFindings.rationale: Complete dissimilarity, exact identity, and unknown extent are clearly separated and confined to the Mark example.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move expressly weighs probabilities, rejects extreme skepticism, and acknowledges the remaining uncertainty without converting it into certainty.

charity.alternative: Historical probability can justify broad continuity despite the loss of exact certainty.
charity.decisiveQualification: Broad continuity leaves the precise extent and location of differences unresolved.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move consistently occupies the middle ground between total discontinuity and exact identity and states what follows from each.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The calibration is exemplary, but the excerpt supplies little affirmative evidence for the probability of broad continuity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the motion-level confidence-gap bridge while conceding the strongest broad-continuity point.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response adopts the strongest probabilistic framing and retains only the qualification that its evidence cannot settle.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly invokes historical probability, rejects the idea that present Mark is wholly unlike Mark's writing, and denies knowledge of exact identity.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The advocate of textual trust bears the burden of providing evidence that the first two centuries of copying and the exemplars behind the earliest manuscripts were sufficiently reliable.
moves.attributionBasis: This argument continues Ehrman's identified closing statement and uses his bridge analogy to frame the burden of proof.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether actual first- and second-century copying and exemplars were reliable enough for trust.
A shared early ancestor still requires evidence concerning that ancestor's quality and relation to earlier copying.
A relative-confidence standard still requires affirmative evidence sufficient to meet the proposed trust threshold.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges the affirmative evidentiary basis for trusting early copyists and exemplars and assigns that demand to the advocate of trust; it contacts the mechanisms but does not disprove their reliability.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it squarely contacts the decisive evidentiary requirement but principally poses questions rather than supplying a contrary transmission model.

precisionFindings.rationale: The burden, first-two-century period, copyist quality, and exemplar quality are expressly and consistently identified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The burden claim appropriately demands evidence for affirmative trust and frames the unresolved historical facts as questions rather than proved unreliability.

charity.alternative: Written branching and early agreement provide indirect evidence of reliable preservation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those mechanisms must still show sufficient reliability during the earliest common transmission period.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Assigning an affirmative evidence burden to a trust claim is coherent, though the bridge analogy does not fix the precise historical threshold.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The missing early evidence motivates the questions, but the move supplies little positive evidence that early copyists or exemplars were actually poor.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and strongly supports the subsidiary burden-standard bridge, reaching the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the pro evidence as potentially relevant while accurately identifying the remaining affirmative burden.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that the advocate of trust bears the burden and asks what evidence establishes skilled early copyists and high-quality exemplars during the first two centuries.

moves.speaker: Daniel B. Wallace
moves.proposition: Historical trust in ancient texts properly rests on probability rather than certainty, because consistently demanding radical certainty would undermine knowledge of ancient literature generally.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the floor to Wallace for his conclusion, and Wallace explicitly answers Ehrman's train illustration.

components.text: The decisive demand is what evidentiary standard the advocate of trust must meet for an ancient text.
Both sides accept probability, leaving the question whether broad historical confidence can support trust.
Ancestral-versus-autographic distinction limits certainty but need not eliminate historically warranted probability.

response.rationale: The reply directly answers the proposed burden by placing New Testament trust within ordinary probabilistic historical reasoning and arguing that radical certainty would undermine ancient-text knowledge generally, though it does not quantify the evidence meeting that standard.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the burden and standard, while leaving the case-specific sufficiency assessment dependent on earlier evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: Probability and extreme skepticism are clearly contrasted, but the precise threshold for historical trust remains unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity of probabilistic rather than certain historical judgment is warranted, with an implicit caveat that standards need not be identical across all texts.

charity.alternative: The advocate of trust bears an affirmative burden concerning unusually early undocumented copying.
charity.decisiveQualification: That burden should demand historically reasonable probability, not certainty unavailable for ancient literature generally.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The consistency argument for probabilistic historical standards is strong, with a bounded bridge needed from general standards to this evidence's sufficiency.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The general comparison with Greco-Roman literature is relevant but compressed and supplies no detailed comparative cases in this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly completes the pro motion-level trust bridge by identifying probability as the appropriate standard.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly retains the affirmative burden while contesting an excessively skeptical standard.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt answers the train analogy by placing all ancient texts on the same evidentiary terrain and warning against a certainty demand that would generalize to Greco-Roman literature.
